one_sentence_story: By testing Henry Molaison ('Patient H.M.') across three days on a mirror-reversed star-tracing box at Montreal/Hartford (1962/1968), Brenda Milner proved the human brain runs separate memory engines: the hippocampus records conscious facts and events ('Knowing What'), while the cerebellum and basal ganglia master physical skills ('Knowing How') even when conscious memory is zero.
so_what_for_you: Trust 'sleep-on-it' physical practice when learning an instrument, sport, typing layout, or surgical skill — your cerebellum and basal ganglia refine motor error curves across days even when Day 1 feels clumsy and unmemorable.

jargon_map.plain: conscious memory for facts and life episodes ('what I ate today', 'when we met') requiring the hippocampus to consolidate
unconscious motor and habit skill ('riding a bike', 'mirror-star tracing') stored in basal ganglia, motor cortex, and cerebellum
jargon_map.analogy: muscle-circuit autopilot that improves across days without needing journal entries

jargon_map.plain: tracing inside a narrow double-bordered 5-pointed star while viewing your hand ONLY in a vertical mirror behind an occlusion shield
jargon_map.analogy: Milner's ingenious puzzle where errors drop from ~30 to ~1 across 3 days

jargon_map.plain: inability to consolidate new conscious declarative memories after bilateral hippocampal damage
jargon_map.analogy: living in an intelligent, polite present without saving new chapters

jargon_map.plain: gradual transfer of episodic memories from temporary hippocampal indexing into long-term neocortical networks
jargon_map.analogy: why H.M. kept his 1930s childhood despite losing his hippocampi in 1953
